summary: Defines requirements and a framework for using GMPLS in multi-region and multi-layer networks, where several switching technologies are controlled together. A region is a switching technology domain and a multi-layer network may have one or several. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5212 describes requirements for controlling networks that use more than one switching technology or data-plane layer. It explains how a GMPLS control plane can coordinate these layers, while leaving protocol solutions to other documents.

subtitle: Requirements for one GMPLS control plane to manage multiple switching regions and network layers.

tldr.problem: Networks with packet, Layer 2, time-division, wavelength, or fiber switching may need separate control arrangements for each technology.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a framework and functional requirements for a single GMPLS control-plane instance to manage multiple layers or switching regions.
tldr.outcome: The document sets requirements rather than protocol solutions. It covers routing, traffic engineering, resource use, operations, and management across layers.

today: RFC 5212 is Informational and was published in July 2008. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Multi-Layer Control Means
sections.content:
GMPLS extends MPLS to support packet, Layer 2, TDM, wavelength, and fiber switching. A region is a domain using one switching type; a layer is a data-plane switching granularity. Several layers can exist within one region.

A multi-layer network (MLN) contains multiple data-plane layers controlled by one GMPLS instance. A multi-region network (MRN) supports at least two switching types under one instance. An MRN is a type of MLN, but an MLN can have multiple layers of the same switching type.
sections.plainLanguage: An MLN has multiple data-plane layers under one GMPLS control plane. An MRN is an MLN that uses more than one switching type.

sections.title: Switching Capabilities and Layer Boundaries
sections.content:
An Interface Switching Capability (ISC) describes the switching type supported by a link interface. The RFC names PSC, L2SC, TDM, LSC, and FSC. A multi-switching-type node may be simplex, with different capabilities on separate interfaces, or hybrid, with multiple capabilities on one interface and internal adjustment between them.

A lower-layer Label Switched Path (LSP) can be advertised as a traffic-engineering link for an upper layer. Such a Forwarding Adjacency LSP can carry higher-layer LSPs. A collection of lower-layer links or paths can form a Virtual Network Topology (VNT), which presents available connectivity to the upper layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Interfaces advertise which switching types they support. A lower-layer path can be presented to an upper layer as a traffic-engineering link.

sections.title: Routing and Resource Requirements
sections.content:
Path computation must handle combinations of single- and multi-switching-type nodes and account for adjustment resources at hybrid nodes. The routing design must scale as node, link, LSP, layer, and switching-capability counts grow. It must also permit filtering traffic-engineering information and working with partial information.

The framework calls for stable VNT changes, minimal disruption when lower-layer paths change, and inheritance of relevant LSP attributes such as bandwidth, protection, and shared-risk information. It also requires policies to control resource use and protection against destabilizing rapid setup and teardown of LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: The control plane must find paths across switching types, use resources efficiently, and limit disruption when the network changes. Operators need policies for how lower-layer paths are created, changed, and released.

sections.title: Verification, Management, and Operations
sections.content:
Lower-layer LSPs may need verification before an upper layer uses them. The document says these checks depend on the data technology, but GMPLS protocols should coordinate their use.

Management can be separate for each layer or coordinated across layers. When different administrative domains operate different layers, they may share limited resource and alarm information. End-to-end OAM must operate across layer boundaries, and the client layer must receive relevant server-layer status, errors, and alarms subject to policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators may manage each layer separately or coordinate management across layers. Monitoring must work across the full path, with policies governing which information crosses administrative boundaries.

sections.title: Security Across Administrative Boundaries
sections.content:
The architecture adds no security requirements beyond the general GMPLS architecture. However, when different administrative domains operate different layers, operators need to consider security for LSP setup, triggered lower-layer paths, and VNT management.

The RFC identifies a tradeoff between sharing enough information for multi-layer traffic engineering and protecting information belonging to each domain. It expects solution documents to analyze the security issues introduced by protocol extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Separate operators may need to share some information to coordinate paths. They must decide how to balance that need with keeping domain information confidential.
